question: An analyst breaks a market review into six stages and feeds each result straight into the next, reviewing nothing until the final report is written. What is the greatest risk?
options: A) A mistake in an early stage is carried into every later stage, and the final report is built on top of it.
B) Later stages will repeat wording from earlier ones, so the finished report reads as somewhat repetitive.
C) The six stages will take longer in total than simply asking for the whole market review in one single request.
D) The final report will be longer than the audience wants, because every stage adds material of its own.
correct_answers: A) A mistake in an early stage is carried into every later stage, and the final report is built on top of it.
explanations: Correct. In a chained breakdown each stage treats the previous output as settled fact. A misread figure or a wrong assumption at stage two is not questioned again, and by stage six it is woven through the analysis and expensive to unpick.
Repetition across stages is a tidying problem that a final editing pass resolves, and it does not affect whether the conclusions hold.
Staged work does take more elapsed time, but that cost is the point of the approach and is small next to acting on a flawed report.
Length is easily controlled by stating limits, and an overlong report is a presentation issue rather than a correctness one.
